overview.title: A 20,001-parameter linear bag-of-words classifier
overview.main_topic: Building, summarizing and starting to train a single-Dense-layer logistic-regression classifier on multi-hot IMDb vectors, with EarlyStopping
overview.central_idea: Each review is a 20,000-dimensional presence vector. A model with one Dense(1, sigmoid) layer, which is logistic regression, assigns one weight per vocabulary word plus a bias, 20,001 parameters in total. It is compiled with Adam and binary crossentropy and trained with an EarlyStopping callback that monitors val_loss with patience 2 and restores the best weights.
overview.importance: This model is the baseline that every later model in chapter 14 is compared against. Wrapping it in `build_linear_classifier` lets the bigram model (p.427–428) reuse it unchanged.
learning_objectives: Write a reusable model-building function with the Functional API
Explain why a Dense(1, sigmoid) layer on multi-hot input is a linear (logistic-regression) bag-of-words model
Derive the 20,001 parameter count and the 78.13 KB size in the summary
Configure EarlyStopping with monitor, patience and restore_best_weights
prerequisites: Sigmoid and binary crossentropy for binary classification (chapter 4)

paragraphs.what_it_says: The next step is a very simple linear model, and the model-building code is saved as a function so it can be used again later.
paragraphs.what_it_means: 'Linear' means the output score is a weighted sum of the inputs (before the sigmoid). The function will be called again with a different vocabulary size for the bigram model.

paragraphs.excerpt: This model is dead simple. We have only 20,001 parameters, one for each
paragraphs.what_it_says: The model is dead simple: only 20,001 parameters, one per vocabulary word and one bias. It is trained with the EarlyStopping callback first covered in chapter 7, which stops training when the validation loss stops improving and restores the weights from the best epoch.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each weight is the learned sentiment value of one word. EarlyStopping removes the need to guess the right number of epochs: training stops after val_loss has failed to improve for 'patience' consecutive epochs, and the model is reset to its best epoch.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: A model this small trains quickly and is hard to overfit badly (p.425). EarlyStopping with restore_best_weights makes sure that the model evaluated on the test set is the best one on validation, not the last one.
paragraphs.technical_idea: With patience=2, if the best val_loss occurs at epoch k, training stops at the end of epoch k+2 at the latest (or at epoch 10) and the weights of epoch k are restored.

concepts.name: Logistic regression (linear classifier)
concepts.definition: A model that computes $\sigma(w^\top x + b)$, one Dense unit with a sigmoid, and outputs the probability of the positive class.
concepts.intuition: Add up the votes of the words present, then squash the total into a probability.
concepts.technical: Here $x\in\{0,1\}^{20000}$, $w\in\mathbb{R}^{20000}$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}$. It is trained with binary crossentropy, so it is exactly logistic regression on bag-of-words features.
concepts.significance: It is the 'bag-of-words regression model' of Listings 14.13–14.15 and gets about 88% test accuracy (p.426).
concepts.example: If 'superb' has a large positive weight and 'boring' a large negative weight, a review containing both is decided by their weights plus everything else present.
concepts.misconception: That 'regression' in the listing titles means it predicts a continuous target. Logistic regression is a classifier; the name is historical.

concepts.name: EarlyStopping callback
concepts.definition: A callback that monitors a validation metric and stops training once it stops improving, optionally restoring the best weights.
concepts.intuition: Stop studying once your practice-test scores stop getting better, and go back to the version of your notes that scored best.
concepts.significance: It automatically selects the number of epochs for this and later chapter 14 models.
concepts.example: If val_loss is lowest at epoch 4 and then rises at epochs 5 and 6, training stops after epoch 6 and the epoch-4 weights are restored.
concepts.misconception: That without restore_best_weights you get the best model. By default the final weights are those of the last epoch run.

concepts.name: Dense layer parameter count
concepts.definition: A Dense layer with $n_{in}$ inputs and $n_{out}$ units has $n_{in}\cdot n_{out} + n_{out}$ parameters.
concepts.intuition: One weight per input–unit connection, plus one bias per unit.
concepts.significance: It explains the number in the model summary.
concepts.example: For the bigram model with 30,000 tokens: 30,001 (p.428).
concepts.misconception: That the InputLayer has parameters. It has 0.

concepts.name: Model-building function with the Functional API
concepts.definition: Wrapping keras.Input → layers → keras.Model → compile in a Python function so the same architecture can be rebuilt with different settings.
concepts.intuition: A recipe card you can reuse with a different-sized pan.
concepts.technical: build_linear_classifier(max_tokens, name) returns a compiled model.
concepts.significance: It allows a fair comparison of unigram and bigram inputs.
concepts.misconception: That calling the function twice returns the same trained model. Each call creates new, untrained weights.

math.title: The linear bag-of-words classifier

variables.meaning: The 20,000-dimensional multi-hot vector of a review.
Weight vector, one weight per vocabulary word (20,000).
Predicted probability that the review is positive.

math.operations: Dot product, add the bias, apply the sigmoid.
math.purpose: Map a review's word set to a probability of positive sentiment.
math.interpretation: Since x is 0/1, $w^\top x$ is just the sum of the weights of the words that are present.
math.intuition: Each present word nudges the score up or down by its weight.
math.numerical_example: Suppose a review contains only three in-vocabulary words with weights 1.2 ('great'), −0.4 ('long') and 0.1 ('film'), and $b=-0.2$. Then $z=0.7$ and $\hat y=\sigma(0.7)\approx 0.67$, so it is predicted positive.

math.title: Parameter count and memory
math.interpretation: The whole model fits in about 78 KiB.
math.intuition: Smaller than a typical web image.
math.numerical_example: 80,004 / 1024 = 78.13, the value Keras reports as KB (strictly KiB).

math.title: Binary crossentropy loss
math.operations: Negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli outcome, averaged over the batch.
math.purpose: The training objective set in compile().
math.interpretation: Confident wrong predictions are penalized heavily.
math.intuition: The loss is −log of the probability the model gave to the correct answer.
math.numerical_example: With y=1: $\hat y=0.67$ gives 0.40, and $\hat y=0.1$ gives 2.30.

code.title: Building a bag-of-words regression model
code.original_code:
def build_linear_classifier(max_tokens, name):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(max_tokens,))
    outputs = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(inputs)
    model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name=name)
    model.compile(
        optimizer="adam",
        loss="binary_crossentropy",
        metrics=["accuracy"],
    )
    return model

model = build_linear_classifier(max_tokens, "bag_of_words_classifier")
code.what_it_does: Defines a function that builds and compiles a one-layer sigmoid classifier for vocabulary-length inputs, and instantiates it for the 20,000-token bag-of-words data.

deeper.title: Reading the trained weights
deeper.body: Beyond the book: because the model is linear on word-presence features, you can interpret it directly. Get `w = model.layers[-1].get_weights()[0][:, 0]` and the vocabulary from `text_vectorization.get_vocabulary()`, then sort. The most negative weights are typically words like 'worst', 'waste' and 'awful', and the most positive ones words like 'excellent' and 'perfect'. This kind of interpretability is part of why the authors chose word tokens, so that 'our weights correspond to actual English words' (p.426).

deeper.title: Why 'regression' for a classifier?
deeper.body: The listing captions say 'bag-of-words *regression* model' while the function is named `build_linear_classifier`. Our reading is that the authors mean logistic regression: a linear regression of the log-odds, $\log\frac{\hat y}{1-\hat y} = w^\top x + b$, turned into a classifier by the sigmoid. Both names describe the same model.

takeaways: Each review is a 20,000-dimensional presence vector.
build_linear_classifier is a one-layer sigmoid model: logistic regression on bag-of-words features.

questions.question: If max_tokens were 30,000, how many parameters would build_linear_classifier produce?
questions.explanation: One weight per input feature plus one bias. This matches the bigram model on p.428.

questions.question: What does restore_best_weights=True do in the EarlyStopping callback?
options: Saves the model to disk at each epoch
Restores the weights from the epoch with the best monitored val_loss when training stops
Re-initializes the weights when the loss increases
Lowers the learning rate when progress stalls
questions.answer: Restores the weights from the epoch with the best monitored val_loss when training stops
questions.explanation: As the page says, it restores the weights from the best epoch. Saving to disk is ModelCheckpoint, re-initializing is not a Keras behavior, and lowering the learning rate is ReduceLROnPlateau.

questions.question: Why is the 78.13 KB in the model summary consistent with 20,001 parameters?
questions.answer: 20,001 float32 values × 4 bytes = 80,004 bytes, and 80,004 / 1024 ≈ 78.13 KB.
questions.explanation: Keras reports sizes in units of 1024 bytes.

questions.question: Why does the book call this model 'linear' even though it has a sigmoid activation?
questions.answer: The pre-activation score is a linear (affine) function $w^\top x + b$ of the inputs. The sigmoid is a monotonic squashing at the output, so the decision boundary $w^\top x + b = 0$ is a hyperplane.
questions.explanation: There are no hidden layers or nonlinear feature interactions, so the model is logistic regression.

questions.question: Why is the model-building code wrapped in a function?
options: Functions train faster than inline code
So the same architecture can be reused later, for example with a different vocabulary size
Because keras.Model must be created inside a function
questions.answer: So the same architecture can be reused later, for example with a different vocabulary size
questions.explanation: The page says it is saved as a function 'so we can use it again later' (the bigram model on p.428). Wrapping does not affect speed, Keras has no such requirement, and each call creates new weights rather than shared ones.

questions.question: With patience=2 and epochs=10, suppose val_loss is lowest at epoch 3 and never improves afterwards. At which epoch does training stop, and which weights does the model end with?
questions.answer: It stops after epoch 5 (two epochs without improvement) and ends with the epoch-3 weights.
questions.explanation: Patience counts consecutive non-improving epochs (4 and 5), and restore_best_weights reloads epoch 3.

questions.question: Can you explain how one weight of this model relates to one specific English word?
questions.answer: Weight i multiplies input i, which is 1 exactly when vocabulary word i is in the review. So weight i is that word's additive contribution to the log-odds of a positive review.
questions.explanation: This is why the authors value word-level tokens for this model (p.426).
